scenes.title: Why this matters
scenes.direction: Define module and standard library through Asha's problem, with the Chapter 10 callback.

visual.heading: Why this matters
visual.label: The big picture
items: A **module** is a Python file whose functions other programs can use.
Write `with_tax()` once. Fix it once. Every program gets the fix.
The **standard library** is the set of modules that comes with Python. You met `random` in Chapter 10.

segments.say: A module is a Python file whose functions other programs can use. Write with tax once, fix it once, and every program gets the fix.
Python also comes with a large set of modules, already written and tested. It is called the standard library. You met one in Chapter 10: random.

scenes.title: The idea: importing
scenes.direction: Teach importing with the diagram, then the three import forms, then the toolbox analogy and where it stops working. Then a quiz and a breather.

visual.heading: One file, many programs
visual.label: The idea
body: **Importing** makes a module's functions available in your program.
visual.pre:
cafe_tools.py               day_report.py
+------------------+        +----------------------------+
| def with_tax()   | <----- | import cafe_tools          |
| def money()      |        | cafe_tools.with_tax(4.0)   |
+------------------+        +----------------------------+
   written once               used here, and in any other
                              program in the same folder

segments.say: Importing makes a module's functions available in your program. Python finds the module file, runs it once, and gives you a name for it.

visual.heading: Three ways to import
visual.label: The idea
rows: You want to see where each function comes from.
You use one or two functions often.
The module name is long; `m` is an alias.

segments.say: There are three common ways to import. Import math keeps the module name in front: math dot ceil.
From math import ceil brings only that one function in, so you call it on its own.
And import math as m gives the module a short name. A short name like this is called an alias.

visual.heading: A module is like a toolbox
visual.label: Analogy
items: `import` takes the whole toolbox to your table.
You still name the tool you want: `math.ceil`.
Where it stops working: Python runs the whole module file when it imports it.

segments.say: Think of a module as a toolbox on a shelf. Import takes the whole box to your table.
You still say which tool you want, as in math dot ceil.
Where the comparison stops working: Python runs the whole module file when it imports it. So a print at the bottom of that file runs too.

visual.question: After `from math import ceil`, which call works?
visual.explain: From ... import brings in only `ceil`, so you call it on its own.

segments.say: Quick check. After from math import ceil, which call works?

after.say: C. Ceil on its own. From import brings in only that one function, not the name math.

items: A module is a Python file you can import.
Three ways: import, from import, import as.
Importing runs the whole file once.

segments.say: Take a breather. Next, Asha imports her first standard module.

scenes.title: Steps 1 and 2: Import a standard module
scenes.direction: Teach ceil and floor, ask what lines 7 and 8 print. Then the three import forms side by side.

visual.heading: Step 1: Boxes of biscuits
visual.hidden_text: Predict the output before it appears.

segments.say: Step 1. Asha orders biscuits in boxes of 12, and she needs 40. Line 2 imports the math module.
Line 6 divides. Line 7 uses math dot ceil, which rounds up to the next whole number. Line 8 uses math dot floor, which rounds down.

after.say: 4 and 3. 40 divided by 12 is 3.33, so ceil rounds up to 4 boxes, and floor rounds down to 3.
Line 9 prints the square root of 49: 7.0. The dot means: the function that lives in the math module.

visual.heading: Step 2: Three imports, one function
visual.hidden_text: Run it to see the output.

segments.say: Step 2. Lines 2 to 4 import in the three ways from the table. Lines 6 to 8 call the same function in those three ways.
All three print 3. In your own programs, pick one style, so readers are not confused.

scenes.title: Step 3: Your own module
scenes.direction: Teach the module file and the main guard, run the module itself, then ask what an importing program prints. Then from-import, a quiz and a breather.

visual.heading: Step 3: Asha's own module
visual.hidden_text: Run it to see the output.

segments.say: Step 3. Asha moves her tools into their own file, cafe tools dot p y. The name of a module is its file name without dot p y.
It holds with tax and money, each with a docstring.
Lines 12 to 15 are test lines, under a special if. Python gives every file a hidden variable called name, with two underscores on each side.
When you run the file itself, that variable holds the text main. When another program imports the file, it holds the module's name instead.
Asha runs the module itself, so the test lines run: two times True.

visual.heading: Another program imports it
visual.hidden_text: Predict the output before it appears.

segments.say: Now a second program, in the same folder, imports the module on line 2.
Line 4 calls cafe tools dot with tax, with 4.0. Line 6 shows the result with money.

ask.question: What does this program print? Do the module's test lines appear?

after.say: 4.4, then 4.40. And no test lines. The module was imported, so its name was not main, and the if skipped them.

segments.say: A third program uses from import, so it calls with tax and money on their own.
The loop prints three prices with tax: 3.85, 4.40 and 3.03. One copy of with tax, used by two programs.
Python looks for cafe tools in the folder of the program you run. So keep your module next to the programs that import it.

visual.question: When do the lines under `if __name__ == "__main__":` run?
options: Every time another program imports the file
Only when you run that file itself
visual.explain: Run directly, the file's name is main. Imported, it is the module's name.

segments.say: Quick check. When do the lines under the main guard run?

after.say: B. Only when you run that file itself. When it is imported, the guard skips them.

items: A module's name is its file name without `.py`.
Keep the module next to its programs.
The main guard hides test lines on import.

segments.say: Breather. Relax your shoulders. Next, two more standard modules: one for time, and one for file names.

scenes.title: Steps 4 and 5: Times and file names
scenes.direction: Teach timedelta, ask what line 7 prints. Teach Path parts, ask what lines 6 and 7 print. Then a quiz.

visual.heading: Step 4: Opening hours with timedelta
visual.hidden_text: Predict the output before it appears.

segments.say: Step 4. The datetime module works with time. A time delta is a length of time. Line 2 imports it.
Line 4: the cafe opens 8 hours after midnight. Line 5: it stays open for 9 hours and 30 minutes. Line 6 adds the two lengths.

after.say: Closes at 17:30:00. Python carries the minutes into hours for you.
Line 8: total seconds gives the length in seconds. Divided by 60, that is 570.0 minutes.

visual.heading: Step 5: File names with pathlib
visual.hidden_text: Predict the output before it appears.

segments.say: Step 5. Pathlib builds file names, without touching any file. A path is the address of a file: its folders and its name.
Line 4 joins a folder and a file name. Here, the forward slash joins the parts. It does not divide.
Name is the whole file name. Stem is the name without its ending. Suffix is the ending.

after.say: Monday, then dot t x t. Line 5 printed the whole name, monday dot t x t.
Windows writes paths with backslashes. So line 8, as posix, shows the path with forward slashes on every system.

visual.question: `Path("menus") / "winter.txt"`. What is its `suffix`?
visual.explain: The suffix is the ending of the file name, with its dot.

segments.say: Quick check. A path joins menus and winter dot t x t. What is its suffix?

after.say: D. Dot t x t. The suffix is the ending. Winter would be the stem.

scenes.title: See the outcome: the day report
scenes.direction: Return to the mission. Walk the imports and lines 7 to 11, ask what line 13 prints, reveal, then hand over to the AI feature.

visual.heading: Mission complete: the day report
visual.hidden_text: Predict the report before it appears.

segments.say: Back to the mission. Lines 2 to 5 put every import at the top, as the style guide asks: three standard modules, then Asha's own.
Line 8 adds tax to each sale with with tax, in a comprehension from Chapter 14, and sum adds the results.
Line 9 rounds up the biscuit boxes, line 10 adds the opening hours, and line 11 builds the report's file name. It does not save a file yet.

after.say: Total: 11.28. That is 3.85, plus 4.40, plus 3.03: the three prices from step 3.
Then 4 boxes, closing at 17:30, and the file name. No copy of with tax anywhere. Mission complete!
Now Asha wants one more tool for her module: how many boxes to order. She builds it with an AI assistant, one stage at a time.

scenes.title: Work with AI: six stages, one function
scenes.direction: Teach the skill. One conversation per stage, all about boxes_needed. Write: her own version and the AI's false claim. Generate: round. Test: two FAIL. Debug: missing import. Improve: an invented function.

visual.heading: This chapter's AI skill: check the documentation
visual.label: Before you start
items: Ask AI which standard module and function fit a task.
Find that function in the official documentation at docs.python.org.
Run it on your own test cases. Never paste private data.

segments.say: This chapter's AI skill: ask an AI which standard module fits a task.
Then find that function in the official documentation, at docs dot python dot org, and run it on your own test cases.

messages.text: I order biscuits in boxes of 12, and I always round up. Which standard module and function do this? Give the exact names and one example. I will check the official documentation.
The `math` module. `math.ceil(x)` returns the smallest whole number that is greater than or equal to x. For example, `math.ceil(3.2)` is `4`.
I found `ceil` on the `math` page of docs.python.org. Its description matches yours.

segments.say: Stage 1: plan. Asha describes the task: boxes of 12, always round up. She asks for the exact module and function, and says she will check them.
The AI names the math module and math dot ceil, with an example.
Asha opens the math page of the official documentation and finds ceil, with the same meaning.

messages.text: First I wrote my own version, without any module. Do not change it. Does it give the same result as a `math.ceil` version for every number of biscuits?
Yes. Both versions always give the same number of boxes.

segments.say: Stage 2: write. Before using the module, Asha writes her own version: double slash, then plus 1. For 40 biscuits, it gives 4.
She asks the AI whether her version always matches a ceil version. The AI says yes, always.

visual.heading: Asha tests two numbers
visual.hidden_text: Predict the output before it appears.

segments.say: Asha tests two numbers: 40, and 24, which divides exactly. Line 5 is her version. Line 6 uses ceil.

ask.question: The AI says both versions always match. Is it right?

after.say: No. For 24 biscuits, her version orders 3 boxes, and ceil orders 2. Her version adds a box even when nothing is left over.
The AI missed her bug. A number that divides exactly found it.

visual.heading: Generate: a function for the module

messages.text: Write `boxes_needed(biscuits, per_box=12)` for my module. It must round up. Add a docstring, and tell me exactly what `boxes_needed(40)` returns.

segments.say: Stage 3: generate. Asha asks for boxes needed, with a docstring, and asks exactly what it returns for 40 biscuits.
The AI writes the function, and says it returns 4.

visual.heading: The AI's function, before Asha runs it
visual.hidden_text: Predict the output before it appears.

segments.say: Here is the AI's function. Line 4 divides, then calls round, from Chapter 2. Line 6 asks for 40 biscuits.

ask.question: The AI says `boxes_needed(40)` returns 4. Is it right?

after.say: No. It prints 3. Round goes to the nearest whole number, so 3.33 becomes 3. Asha would be 4 biscuits short.

messages.text: Your version gives 3 for 40 biscuits. Here are my test cases: 40 gives 4, 24 gives 2, 1 gives 1, 0 gives 0. Is any case missing?
Your cases cover a remainder, an exact division, one biscuit and zero. That is a good set. Run them on every version.

segments.say: Stage 4: test. Asha writes four cases with the result she expects: a remainder, an exact division, one biscuit, and zero. She asks the AI if any case is missing.
The AI says the set is good, and tells her to run it on every version.

visual.heading: The four cases, on the AI's version

segments.say: Line 5 holds the cases, in a dictionary: biscuits, and the expected boxes. The loop prints pass or FAIL for each one.
On the AI's version, 40 and 1 fail. Round never rounds 1 twelfth up to a whole box.

visual.heading: Debug: the cause before the fix

messages.text: I changed it to `math.ceil` and got this error. First explain the cause and the line. Then show the smallest fix.

segments.say: Stage 5: debug. Asha changes round to math dot ceil, runs it, and Python stops. She pastes the code and the full error, and asks for the cause first.

messages.text: I changed it to `math.ceil` and got this error. First explain the cause and the line. Then show the smallest fix.

It is a `NameError` on line 4. The file uses `math`, but it never imports it.
The fix: add `import math` as the first line of the file.

segments.say: The AI names line 4: the file uses math, but never imports it. The error even asks: did you forget to import math? The fix: add import math at the top.

visual.heading: Every case, again, after the fix

segments.say: Line 2 imports math, and line 5 uses ceil. Asha runs every case again.
All four pass, including the exact division and zero.

messages.text: My function passes every case. Suggest one improvement, with one reason. Name the documentation page for any function you use.
Use `math.ceildiv(biscuits, per_box)`. It divides and rounds up in one step, so the code is shorter. You will find it on the `math` module page.

segments.say: Stage 6: improve. Asha asks for one improvement, and for the documentation page of any function it uses.
The AI suggests math dot ceil div. It divides and rounds up in one step, and the AI says it is on the math page.

visual.heading: Checking the suggestion
visual.hidden_text: Predict what happens before it appears.

segments.say: Asha searches the math page for ceil div, and does not find it. To be sure, she runs one line.

after.say: No. Attribute Error: module math has no attribute ceil div. Here, attribute means a name inside the module. That function does not exist.
The AI made it up, and named a real page for it. Asha keeps math dot ceil. Her four cases still pass.

visual.question: An AI names a function you have never seen. What do you do first?
options: Find it in the official documentation, then run it
Use it, because the AI checked it
Ask the AI if it is sure
visual.explain: The documentation and a real run decide, not the AI.

segments.say: Quick check. An AI names a function you have never seen. What do you do first?

after.say: A. Find it in the official documentation, then run it.

items: Find every function in the documentation.
Test a number that divides exactly.
Run every case after every fix.

segments.say: Breather. Asha caught three AI problems: a false promise about her own code, round instead of ceil, and a function that does not exist.

scenes.title: Common mistakes
scenes.direction: Mistake 1 is a spot-it question on a module name. Mistake 2 calls back to the quiz. Mistake 3 shows a file named random.py. Mistake 4 is a predict question on a module without the guard.

visual.heading: Mistake 1: your turn to spot it
visual.hidden_text: Find the problem before the answer appears.

segments.say: Now you try. Line 2 imports Asha's module. Compare it with step 3.

after.say: The name is cafe tool, without the s. Python looks for a file with exactly that name, finds none, and stops with a Module Not Found Error.
after.heading: Mistake 1: a typing error in the module name

after.say: Newer versions of Python even suggest the right name. The fix: spell it like the file.

visual.heading: Mistake 2: a function without its module name

segments.say: Mistake 2 is the quick check from the idea section, in reverse. After import math, the full name is math dot ceil. Ceil on its own is not defined.
The fix: write math dot ceil, or import it with from math import ceil.
Mistake 3. Asha saved a test file called random dot p y, next to this program. Now import random finds her file first, not Python's module.
The first output line comes from her test file. Then her file has no rand int, so Python stops with an Attribute Error.
Python 3.13 and newer add advice: consider renaming the file. The fix: rename it, for example to random test dot p y.

visual.heading: Mistake 4: a module without the guard

segments.say: Mistake 4. This module has a test line at the bottom, line 5, with no main guard. Run on its own, it prints its test line.

visual.heading: A program imports it
visual.hidden_text: Predict the output before it appears.

segments.say: Another program imports money from that module, and prints the tea price.

after.say: Two lines: the module's test line, then the tea. Importing runs the whole file, so the test line appears in every program that imports it.
There is no error, which makes it easy to miss. The fix: put test lines under the main guard.

items: Spell the module like its file.
Never name a file like a standard module.
Test lines go under the main guard.

visual.heading: Recap
visual.label: What you learned
items: A module is a Python file whose functions other programs can import.
The standard library is the set of modules that comes with Python.
`import math`, `from math import ceil` and `import math as m` all work.
Importing runs the whole file once. The main guard keeps test lines quiet.
`math.ceil()` rounds up, `timedelta` adds times, `Path` reads file names.
Find every function an AI names in the documentation, then run it.

segments.say: Let's recap. A module is a Python file whose functions other programs can import, and the standard library is the set of modules that comes with Python.
There are three ways to import. Importing runs the whole file once, and the main guard keeps test lines quiet.
Ceil rounds up, time delta adds times, and Path reads file names. And when an AI names a function, find it in the documentation, then run it.

visual.question: After `import math as m`, which call works?
visual.explain: The alias `m` is the only name the import creates.

segments.say: One last check. After import math as m, which call works?

after.say: C. M dot square root. The alias m is the only name that import creates.
